units.text: Rangeland abandonment may occur due to changes in global markets or mismanagement of resources (Gellrich and Zimmermann, 2007) but may also follow strategic developments. Pertaining to the latter, a recent large-scale example is the abandonment of extensive areas of semi-desert Nama-Karoo rangeland in South Africa for the development of the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) project, as part of the world’s largest radio telescope (Taylor, 2012). Consequently, after centuries of farming, ca. 13,000 sheep are no longer grazing the ca. 130,000 ha of land used for the SKA development. The impacts of rangeland abandonment on native biota and ecosystem functions in this semi-desert are unknown, but especially relevant as the often-overexploited, arid regions of the world take decades to recover after disturbances (Allen et al., 1995; Steed et al., 2018).

At each plot, four pitfall traps were placed in a square with at least 100 m separation to minimize trap interference between 08:00 and 12:00 in the morning (Larsen and Forsyth, 2005). Therefore, sampling effort for this study was: 3 x grazing regimes x 3 landscape features x 8 plots x 4 traps x 2 seasons = 476 traps in total. Traps consisted of plastic cups with openings of 5.7 cm and depths of 9.0 cm that were buried with their rims level with the soil surface (Pryke et al., 2013). As different taxa are attracted to different sources (Davis et al., 2020), each trap per plot was baited with a different bait source. Baits included pig dung (omnivore), cow dung (pats), sheep dung (pellets), and rotten chicken livers (carrion) (Pryke et al., 2013). Dung was collected from abattoirs and thoroughly mixed to create consistency in volatiles. Bait balls consisted of 150 g of dung or carrion that were placed into separate breathable material bags, frozen to kill pathogens and to ensure freshness and consistency in dung volatiles between different sampling days and suspended over the pitfall traps using wire (Pryke et al., 2016).

Ten traits were selected to define the functional identity of the species collected here. In addition to (1) nesting strategy (dung relocation behaviour) and (2) dry mass (as proxy for the dung mass needed for normal larval development) we also measured (3) the total length of the beetle (using digital callipers) from the tip of the abdomen to the tip of the clypeus, as larger beetles can manipulate more dung than smaller individuals (Nervo et al., 2014). (4) Activity was recorded from the literature (Davis et al., 2020) as nocturnal or diurnal (coded as 1—diurnal or 0—nocturnal for analyses). Diet preferences of the dung beetles in the region can be separated into coprophagous (dung), necrophagous (carrion), or generalists that will utilise more than one source (Davis et al., 2020). Coprophagous taxa can be further subdivided into those that prefer dung from non-ruminal vertebrates, ruminal vertebrates, or omnivorous vertebrates. (5) Species were therefore scored one point per dung type they are able to utilise (carrion, ruminal dung, omnivorous dung, and non-ruminant dung), and then, depending on how many sources a particular dung beetle species utilized, as indicated in the literature (Davis et al., 2020) and our own collections, a score between 1 and 4 was assigned to each species. A larger head area indicates that a beetle can manipulate relatively larger quantities of dung (Nervo et al., 2014; Tonelli et al., 2018). We therefore calculated (6) the head surface area of each dung beetle species, using Image J software (ImageJ2, National Institute of Health) after taking photos of dismembered beetles on a background with a standardised grid of 1 mm × 1 mm. Similarly, beetles with larger fore tibia will presumably manipulate dung more easily than those with smaller fore tibia, therefore (7) fore tibial area, as determined using Image J software, was also included in the analyses. Species with longer legs can generally move faster and roll larger dung balls than species with shorter legs (Inward et al., 2011). We therefore measured (8) hind tibia length (mm) using digital callipers. Long-distance dispersal ability of dung beetles is strongly affected by wing load (da Silva and Hern´andez, 2015a). Wing load (9) was calculated from the dry mass data and the area of the hind wings, which were determined using Image J software $( \mathrm{mg/mm^2} )$ . To calculate wing area, the wings were removed before drying of specimens, opened to their full extent, and photographed. Different dung beetle species may differ in terms of which specific months of the year they are active. Therefore, the final trait included was (10) phenology (seasonal activity). Phenology information was sourced from the literature (Davis et al., 2020) and according to our own collections and coded as outlined by Tonelli et al. (2017) for analyses.

A study on dung beetle diversity in a Brazilian semi-arid ecosystem indicated that dung beetle communities in undisturbed areas were species poor in comparison to those that were actively farmed (Liberal et al., 2011). In semi-arid central Spain, Lobo et al. (2006) and Tonelli et al. (2018) found that the abandonment of traditional pastoral systems caused decreased dung beetle diversity. Similarly, Verdú et al. (2007) found that grazing by livestock encouraged dung beetle diversity in Mexico. The difference between these studies and the present one seems to be that dung beetles were able to readily exploit the exotic dung resources produced by livestock in the former. Differences in dung quality and not quantity may therefore be the most important key to disentangle these contrasting patterns (Nependa et al., 2021). To improve conditions for enriched dung beetle diversity and function, reintroductions of native meso-herbivores, such as wildebeest and zebra, should be considered in the abandoned Nama-Karoo areas (Lovegrove and Siegfried, 1993). Increased dung beetle diversity and functional richness will also benefit active farming areas as it improves vegetation development, nutrient cycling, and parasite and pest control (Nichols et al., 2008). Therefore, increased abundance of omnivores, ruminants, and wild herbivores on farms should be encouraged.
